questions.question: Whose tomb, almost untouched after more than 3,000 years, did Howard Carter find in the Valley of the Kings in November 1922?
questions.hint: He became king as a boy of about nine and died at about eighteen or nineteen. The dig was paid for by Lord Carnarvon.
questions.explanation: Tutankhamun ruled Egypt from about 1332 to 1323 BC and was not an important king. Robbers got into his small tomb twice soon after the burial, but later the entrance was buried under rubble and workmen's huts from another king's tomb, and it was forgotten. It held about 5,000 objects, among them the gold mask, which has been in the Grand Egyptian Museum near Cairo since 2025.

image.alt: An old photograph of a small room packed with furniture: a carved couch with animal legs, boxes, chairs and stools, each with a number card.

label.title: The antechamber of the tomb of Tutankhamun

questions.question: This stone, found in Egypt in 1799, carries the same decree in three kinds of writing. It gave scholars the key to Egyptian hieroglyphs. What is it called?
questions.hint: Soldiers of Napoleon's army found it while rebuilding a fort in the Nile delta. The British took it in 1801, and it has been in the British Museum since 1802.
questions.explanation: The stone is named after Rosetta, the town in the delta near which it was found. The decree, of 196 BC, is written in hieroglyphs, in demotic, the everyday Egyptian script, and in Greek. Scholars could read the Greek, and so they had a way into the other two.

image.alt: A slab of black stone, broken at the top and at the corners, covered with three blocks of fine carved writing.

label.artist: Plate from E. A. Wallis Budge, The Rosetta Stone
label.title: The Rosetta Stone

questions.question: "Mesopotamia" is Greek for "the land between the rivers". Which two rivers?
options: The Amu Darya and the Syr Darya
questions.hint: Both rise in the mountains of eastern Turkey. A famous capital city of today stands on one of them.
questions.explanation: Most of Mesopotamia lies in today's Iraq. The rivers made farming possible in a land with little rain, and some of the first cities in the world grew up there more than 5,000 years ago, such as Uruk. The two rivers join before they reach the sea.

questions.question: The Sumerians of Mesopotamia invented one of the first writing systems more than 5,000 years ago. Scribes pressed its signs into wet clay with a cut reed. What is it called?
questions.hint: It began in the city of Uruk as a way of counting grain and animals. It was used for about 3,000 years, and for many different languages.
questions.explanation: The name comes from the Latin "cuneus", a wedge, after the shape of the marks. Hundreds of thousands of clay tablets survive, because clay does not rot and fire only makes it harder. Many of them are receipts, lists and letters.

questions.question: Which king of Babylon, in about 1754 BC, had 282 laws carved on a tall black stone that is now in the Louvre?
questions.hint: At the top of the stone the king stands before Shamash, the god of the sun and of justice. One of his laws says that if a man puts out another man's eye, his own eye shall be put out.
questions.explanation: The Code of Hammurabi is one of the oldest sets of written laws that we can still read. The punishment depended on rank: an eye for an eye between equals, but only a fine if the victim was a commoner. French archaeologists found the stone in the winter of 1901 to 1902 at Susa, in Iran, where an enemy king had carried it off as war booty.

questions.question: For which pharaoh was the Great Pyramid of Giza built, in about 2560 BC?
questions.hint: His father, Sneferu, built the first true pyramids. One of his sons built the second pyramid of Giza, which looks taller because it stands on higher ground.
questions.explanation: The Great Pyramid was about 146 metres high and was the tallest building in the world for about 3,800 years. It is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world that still stands. It was built by Egyptian workers who were housed and fed by the king, not by slaves, as their town and tombs near the site show.

questions.question: Which French scholar announced in 1822 that he could read Egyptian hieroglyphs?
questions.hint: He was 31 and had studied ancient languages since he was a boy, among them Coptic, the last form of Egyptian. The story goes that he ran to his brother's office shouting "I've got it!" and fainted.
questions.explanation: Champollion understood that hieroglyphs are a mix of signs for sounds and signs for ideas. He worked from the Rosetta Stone and from royal names such as Ptolemy, Cleopatra and Ramesses. His rival, the English scientist Thomas Young, had read some signs before him but never the whole system.

questions.question: In 1872 George Smith of the British Museum read a clay tablet of the Epic of Gilgamesh and caused a sensation. It told a story very close to one in the Bible. Which story?
questions.hint: The hero Gilgamesh, looking for a way not to die, meets Utnapishtim, the one man to whom the gods gave eternal life, and asks how he won it.
questions.explanation: Utnapishtim tells how a god warned him of a great flood. He built a boat, took animals on board and, when the boat came to rest on a mountain, sent out a dove, a swallow and a raven to look for land. The tablet, from Nineveh, was written in the seventh century BC, but the story is far older.

image.alt: A piece of a clay tablet in a museum case, broken at the edges and closely covered with small writing in two columns.

label.title: The Flood Tablet: tablet 11 of the Epic of Gilgamesh

questions.question: In about 1259 BC the pharaoh Ramesses II made a peace treaty that is often called the oldest one whose text survives. With which people did he make it?
questions.hint: The two armies had fought a great chariot battle at Kadesh, in Syria, about fifteen years earlier. A copy of the treaty hangs in the United Nations building in New York.
questions.explanation: Both Ramesses and the Hittite king Muwatalli claimed to have won at Kadesh. The treaty was made later with King Hattusili III, and copies from both sides survive: one carved on temple walls in Egypt, and one on clay tablets found at Hattusa, the Hittite capital, in today's Turkey.

image.alt: A coloured print of a temple cut into a cliff: four giant seated statues of a king, half buried in a slope of sand.

label.title: The Great Temple of Abu Simbel

questions.question: Which Assyrian king of the seventh century BC collected a library of many thousands of clay tablets in his palace at Nineveh?
questions.hint: He boasted that, unlike other kings, he could read and write. Stone reliefs from his palace, now in London, show him hunting lions.
questions.explanation: Ashurbanipal ruled from 669 to about 631 BC and was the last great king of Assyria. When Nineveh was burned in 612 BC, the fire baked the clay tablets hard and so preserved them. More than 30,000 tablets and pieces are now in the British Museum, among them the Epic of Gilgamesh.
